paragraphs: The examination of the witnesses began. But we will not tell the story in as much detail as before. We will not dwell on how Nikolay Parfenovitch pressed each witness to give his evidence truthfully and in good conscience, and warned that he would later have to repeat it under oath. Nor will we describe how every witness was made to sign the protocol of his statement, and so on. We will only note that the examination centered chiefly on the question of the three thousand roubles. That is, was the sum Mitya spent here at Mokroe the first time, a month before, three thousand or fifteen hundred? And had he spent three thousand or fifteen hundred yesterday? Alas, all the evidence from every witness turned out to be against Mitya. Not one witness spoke in his favor, and some brought forward new, almost crushing facts that contradicted Mitya’s own story.

The first witness examined was Trifon Borissovitch. He was not in the least abashed as he stood before the lawyers. On the contrary, he had an air of stern, severe indignation toward the accused, which made him seem truthful and dignified. He spoke little and with reserve, waited to be questioned, and answered precisely and deliberately. Firmly and without hesitation he stated that the sum spent a month before could not have been less than three thousand. All the peasants around here, he said, would testify that they had heard Dmitri Fyodorovitch himself mention three thousand. “What a lot of money he flung away on the gypsy girls alone! He wasted a thousand on them alone, I’d say.”
“I don’t think I gave them even five hundred,” Mitya said gloomily. “It’s a pity I didn’t count the money at the time, but I was drunk....”
Mitya was sitting sideways, with his back to the curtains. He listened gloomily, looking sad and worn out, as though he would say:
“Oh, say what you like. It makes no difference now.”

“More than a thousand went on them, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Trifon Borissovitch retorted firmly. “You flung it about at random and they picked it up. They were a rascally, thieving lot, horse-stealers. They’ve been driven away from here, or maybe they’d testify themselves how much they got from you. I saw the sum in your hands myself—count it I didn’t, you wouldn’t let me, that’s true enough—but from the look of it I’d say it was far more than fifteen hundred ... fifteen hundred, indeed! We’ve seen money too. We can judge amounts....”
As for the sum spent yesterday, he stated that Dmitri Fyodorovitch had told him, as soon as he arrived, that he had brought three thousand with him.
“Come now, is that so, Trifon Borissovitch?” Mitya replied. “Surely I didn’t say so positively that I’d brought three thousand?”

“You did say so, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You said it in front of Andrey. Andrey himself is still here. Send for him. And in the hall, when you were treating the chorus, you shouted right out that you would leave your sixth thousand here—that is, counting what you spent before, we must understand. Stepan and Semyon heard it, and Pyotr Fomitch Kalganov was standing beside you at the time too. Maybe he’d remember it....”

The evidence about the “sixth” thousand made an extraordinary impression on the two lawyers. They were delighted with this new way of reckoning: three and three made six, three thousand then and three now made six, that was clear.

They questioned all the peasants Trifon Borissovitch named, Stepan and Semyon, the driver Andrey, and Kalganov. The peasants and the driver confirmed Trifon Borissovitch’s evidence without hesitation. They noted down with particular care Andrey’s account of the conversation he had had with Mitya on the road: “‘Where,’ says he, ‘am I going, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, to heaven or to hell, and will I be forgiven in the next world or not?’”
The psychological Ippolit Kirillovitch heard this with a subtle smile, and ended by recommending that these remarks about where Dmitri Fyodorovitch would go should be “included in the case.”

Kalganov, when called, came in reluctantly, frowning and in a bad temper. He spoke to the lawyers as though he had never met them before in his life, though they were acquaintances he had been meeting every day for a long time. He began by saying that “he knew nothing about it and didn’t want to.” But it came out that he had heard of the “sixth” thousand, and he admitted that he had been standing close by at the moment. As far as he could see, he “didn’t know” how much money Mitya had in his hands. He stated that the Poles had cheated at cards. Under repeated questioning he said that after the Poles had been thrown out, Mitya’s position with Agrafena Alexandrovna had certainly improved, and that she had said she loved him. He spoke of Agrafena Alexandrovna with reserve and respect, as though she were a lady of the best society, and did not once allow himself to call her Grushenka. The young man obviously hated giving evidence, but Ippolit Kirillovitch questioned him at great length, and only from him learned all the details of what made up Mitya’s “romance,” so to speak, on that night. Mitya did not once stop Kalganov. At last they let the young man go, and he left the room in open indignation.

The Poles were examined too. Though they had gone to bed in their room, they had not slept all night. When the police officers arrived they dressed in a hurry and got ready, realizing they would certainly be sent for. They gave their evidence with dignity, though not without some uneasiness. The little Pole turned out to be a retired official of the twelfth class, who had served in Siberia as a veterinary surgeon. His name was Mussyalovitch. Pan Vrublevsky turned out to be an unlicensed dentist. Although Nikolay Parfenovitch put his questions to them as they came in, they both addressed their answers to Mihail Makarovitch, who was standing to one side. In their ignorance they took him for the most important person and the one in command, and they called him “Pan Colonel” at every word. Only after several reproofs from Mihail Makarovitch himself did they grasp that they must direct their answers to Nikolay Parfenovitch alone. It turned out that they could speak Russian quite correctly, apart from their accent on some words. When Pan Mussyalovitch spoke of his relations with Grushenka, past and present, he did so proudly and warmly. Mitya was roused at once and declared that he would not allow the “scoundrel” to speak like that in his presence! Pan Mussyalovitch immediately drew attention to the word “scoundrel” and asked that it be put down in the protocol. Mitya fumed with rage.
“He’s a scoundrel! A scoundrel! You can put that down. And put down, too, that in spite of the protocol I still say he’s a scoundrel!” he cried.

Nikolay Parfenovitch did enter this in the protocol, but he showed the most praiseworthy tact and skill. After sternly reprimanding Mitya, he cut off all further questions about the romantic side of the case and hurried on to what was essential. One piece of the Poles’ evidence roused special interest in the lawyers. In that very room, Mitya had tried to buy off Pan Mussyalovitch, offering him three thousand roubles to give up his claims: seven hundred roubles down, and the remaining two thousand three hundred “to be paid next day in the town.” He had sworn at the time that he did not have the whole sum with him at Mokroe, but that his money was in the town. Mitya said hotly that he had not said he would be sure to pay the rest next day in the town. But Pan Vrublevsky confirmed the statement, and Mitya, after thinking for a moment, admitted with a frown that it must have been as the Poles said, that he had been excited at the time and might indeed have said so.

The prosecutor simply pounced on this piece of evidence. It seemed to establish for the prosecution (and they did in fact build their deduction on it) that half of the three thousand that had come into Mitya’s hands, or some part of it, might really have been left hidden somewhere in the town, or even perhaps somewhere here in Mokroe. This would explain the fact that so baffled the prosecution: only eight hundred roubles had been found on Mitya. That fact, small as it was, had been the one piece of evidence that had so far told to some extent in Mitya’s favor. Now this one piece of evidence in his favor had collapsed. The prosecutor asked where he would have got the remaining two thousand three hundred roubles, since he himself had denied having more than fifteen hundred. Mitya answered confidently that he had meant to offer the “little chap” not money but a formal deed handing over his rights to the village of Tchermashnya, the same rights he had already offered to Samsonov and Madame Hohlakov. The prosecutor actually smiled at the “innocence of this trick.”
“And you imagine he would have accepted such a deed in place of two thousand three hundred roubles in cash?”

“He certainly would have accepted it,” Mitya declared warmly. “Why, look here, he might have grabbed not two thousand but four or six for it. He would have set his lawyers on the job, Poles and Jews, and he might have got not three thousand but the whole property out of the old man.”

Pan Mussyalovitch’s evidence was, of course, entered in the protocol in the fullest detail. Then they let the Poles go. The incident of the cheating at cards was hardly touched on. Nikolay Parfenovitch was too well pleased with them as it was, and did not want to bother them with trifles. Besides, it was nothing but a foolish, drunken quarrel over cards. There had been drinking and disorder enough that night.... So the two hundred roubles stayed in the pockets of the Poles.

Then old Maximov was summoned. He came in timidly, with little steps, looking very disheveled and depressed. All this time he had taken refuge downstairs with Grushenka, sitting dumbly beside her, and “now and then he’d begin blubbering over her and wiping his eyes with a blue check handkerchief,” as Mihail Makarovitch described afterwards. So she had ended up trying to calm and comfort him herself. The old man confessed at once that he had done wrong, that he had borrowed “ten roubles in my poverty” from Dmitri Fyodorovitch, and that he was ready to pay it back. Nikolay Parfenovitch asked him straight out whether he had noticed how much money Dmitri Fyodorovitch held in his hand, since he must have been able to see the sum better than anyone when he took the note from him. Maximov declared, in the most positive manner, that there was twenty thousand.
“Have you ever seen as much as twenty thousand before, then?” Nikolay Parfenovitch asked with a smile.

“Of course I have, not twenty, but seven, when my wife mortgaged my little property. She only let me look at it from a distance, boasting of it to me. It was a very thick bundle, all rainbow-colored notes. And Dmitri Fyodorovitch’s were all rainbow-colored....”

He was not kept long. At last it was Grushenka’s turn. Nikolay Parfenovitch was clearly worried about the effect her appearance might have on Mitya, and he muttered a few words of warning to him. But Mitya bowed his head in silence, giving him to understand “that he would not make a scene.” Mihail Makarovitch himself led Grushenka in. She entered with a stern and gloomy face that looked almost calm, and sat down quietly on the chair Nikolay Parfenovitch offered her. She was very pale, she seemed to be cold, and she wrapped herself closely in her magnificent black shawl. She was suffering from a slight feverish chill—the first sign of the long illness that followed that night. Her grave air, her direct, earnest look and her quiet manner made a very favorable impression on everyone. Nikolay Parfenovitch was even a little bit “fascinated.” He admitted himself, when talking about it afterwards, that only then had he seen “how handsome the woman was.” Though he had seen her several times before, he had always thought of her as something of a “provincial hetaira.” “She has the manners of the best society,” he said enthusiastically, gossiping about her in a circle of ladies. But the ladies received this with real indignation and immediately called him a “naughty man,” to his great satisfaction.
